description:
Faside Estate occupies a commanding ridge near Tranent in East Lothian, roughly midway between Musselburgh and the town itself, and its name carries a documented history stretching back further than almost any other property in this collection. The name itself dates to 1189, when monks from Newbattle Abbey granted this land to Saer de Quincy, who would go on to become the 1st Earl of Winchester, specifically so that he could build a castle here — though local tradition and archaeological evidence both suggest some form of fortification had already occupied this prominent, defensible ridge since as early as the 11th century, well before de Quincy's formal grant.

Ownership in the centuries that followed passed through several hands typical of medieval Scottish landholding disputes: the property belonged at one point to Alexander de Such, before being confiscated by Robert the Bruce, whose consolidation of royal authority in the early 14th century involved exactly this kind of redistribution of contested estates. The Fawside family — whose name is directly reflected in the estate's own — held the property through the 13th and 14th centuries, with specific individuals recorded in the historical record: Thomas de Fawside, a knight, appears in 1376, and William and Gavin of Fawside are both documented in 1476, giving Faside an unusually well-preserved thread of named medieval ownership.

The estate's single most significant historical moment came in 1547, when it found itself overlooking the Battle of Pinkie — a genuinely consequential engagement remembered as the last pitched battle fought between Scotland and England as fully separate nations, before the eventual union of the crowns reshaped the relationship between the two countries. The Duke of Somerset commanded the English forces from a position immediately beside the castle, placing Faside at the literal centre of one of the defining military encounters in Anglo-Scottish history.

A new house was built alongside the older castle structure in 1618, and the estate's fortunes fluctuated considerably in the centuries that followed: it was sold in 1631 to an Edinburgh merchant named Hamilton, and its notable absence from window tax records between 1748 and 1798 — a period when most substantial houses of this kind would be expected to appear in such records — strongly suggests the property stood empty or largely unused for much of the later 18th century. Faside's more recent history has been considerably kinder: the estate was restored in the 1980s and now holds Category B listed status, Scotland's official recognition of buildings of particular architectural or historic interest.

Unlike every other property in this collection, Faside does not operate as a conventional hotel offering individual room bookings. Instead, the estate is rented on an exclusive-use basis for private events, weddings and luxury retreats — meaning a booking secures the entire castle and its grounds for the duration of the stay, rather than a single room within a shared property. This model reflects both the estate's more intimate scale and its positioning toward groups seeking privacy and exclusivity, and prospective visitors should approach Faside with that distinction clearly in mind: there is no day-visit, restaurant or casual dropped-in access here, and current rates and availability are best confirmed directly through the booking link for specific event dates.

faqs.question: Can I book a single room at Faside Estate like a normal hotel?
faqs.answer: No. Faside Estate operates on an exclusive-use rental model rather than as a conventional hotel — a booking secures the entire castle and grounds for private events, weddings or luxury retreats, not an individual room within a shared property. There is no day-visit or casual walk-in access, and current rates for exclusive hire are best confirmed directly through the booking link for specific dates.

faqs.question: What is the Battle of Pinkie, and why is it significant to Faside Estate?
faqs.answer: The Battle of Pinkie, fought in 1547, is remembered as the last pitched battle fought between Scotland and England as fully separate nations before the eventual union of the crowns. Faside Estate directly overlooked the battle, and the Duke of Somerset commanded English forces from a position immediately beside the castle, placing the estate at the centre of this historically significant Anglo-Scottish engagement.

faqs.question: How old is Faside Estate?
faqs.answer: The name Faside dates to 1189, when monks of Newbattle Abbey granted the land to Saer de Quincy, 1st Earl of Winchester, specifically to build a castle. Evidence suggests a fortification may have already stood on this prominent ridge since as early as the 11th century, making Faside's documented history among the longest of any property in this collection.
